title: Matthew 1:18: birth and genesis
english: Verse 18. “Now the birth of Jesus was in this way” (Matthew 1:18). Here the evangelist speaks of his birth, but at the beginning of the Gospel of his genesis. Here he says, “Now the birth of Jesus Christ was in this way”; there, “The book of the genesis of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1). What, then, is the difference between birth and genesis? And how are both said of Christ?

Take this spoken word of ours. By its own nature it cannot be touched or seen; but when it is written in a book and, as it were, takes a body, then it is both seen and handled. So too the Word of God, without flesh and without body, is neither seen nor written in his Godhead; but since he took flesh, he is both seen and written. That is why, since he was made flesh, there is also a book of his genesis.

But the question here is not why he said “book” rather than “vision” or “word”. It is this: what is birth, and what is genesis? Genesis and birth differ. Genesis is the first fashioning, which comes from God. Birth is the succession of one from another, which comes from the sentence of death passed because of the transgression. Again, genesis has incorruption and sinlessness, while birth has liability to suffering and to sin. So the Lord took from genesis its sinlessness, by nature, but did not also take its incorruption; and he took from birth its liability to suffering, but did not also take its liability to sin. In this way he bore the first Adam, undiminished in what belongs to both.

So in Christ's case genesis would not be a passage from not being into being. It would be a road, from existing in the form of God to taking up the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6-7). His birth was twofold: like ours, and beyond ours. To be born of a woman is like ours. To be born not of the will of the flesh or of a man (John 1:13), but of the Holy Spirit, is beyond ours. And this proclaimed in advance the birth to come, which he would grant us from the Spirit.

title: Luke 1:1–2: many undertook; the Church keeps four
english: Verse 1. “Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the things that have been fulfilled among us” (Luke 1:1). The task was too great: for a man to write down the teaching and words of God. So he rightly makes his apology in the preface. Among the people of old many claimed to prophesy. Some of them were false prophets and some were true prophets, and there was a gift, the discerning of spirits, by which the true prophet and the false prophet were told apart. So too now, in the new covenant, many wanted to write Gospels. But the tested money-changers did not approve them all; they chose some of them.

Perhaps the word “undertook” also carries a hidden charge against those who came to the writing of Gospels rashly and without the gift. Matthew did not undertake; he wrote, moved by the Holy Spirit. So did Mark, and John in the same way, and Luke. But those who wrote the Gospel entitled “according to the Egyptians” and the one entitled “of the Twelve” undertook. Basilides even dared to write a Gospel according to Basilides. Many, then, undertook, but the Church of God prefers the four alone.

He did not simply say “believed” but “fulfilled”, bearing witness that what is told cannot be set aside. And he said “things”, to overthrow the heresy of those who say that what was done through the Saviour happened only in appearance. “Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word handed them down to us” (Luke 1:2).
